B

Djoser was the first king of the Third Dynasty (রাজবংি) of Egypt and the first to build

in stone (োথর). Prior to Djoser’s reign (রাজে), tombs (সিামধগুললা) were rectangular

(আয়েলক্ষোযার) monuments (স্মৃমেস্তম্ভ) made of dried (শুযলনা) clay brick (ইি), which

covered (আোমদে) underground (ভূগভেস্থ) passages where the deceased (িৃে) person was

buried (েমেে). For reasons which remain unclear, Djoser’s main official, whose name

was Imhotep (ইিলহালিে), conceived (েমরযেনাযরা) of building a taller, more impressive

tomb for his king by stacking stone slabs (স্তুে) on top of one another, progressively (ধীলর

ধীলর) making them smaller, to form the shape now known as the Step Pyramid. Djoser

is thought to have reigned (রাজে) for 19 years, but some historians (ইমেহাসমবদ) and

scholars (মিক্ষামবদ) attribute (দায়ীযরা) a much longer time for his rule, owing to (যারে)

the number and size of the monuments he built (মনমিে) .

পজাসারমিললনমিিলররেৃেীয়রাজবংলিরপ্রথিরাজাএবংোথরমনিোেযারীপ্রথিবেমক্ত।পজাসালরর

রাজলেরআলগসিামধগুললাশুযলনািামিরইলিরবেমরআয়েলক্ষোযারস্মৃমেস্তম্ভমিল, যািৃেবেমক্তলয

যবরপদওয়ারজনেভূগভেস্থআোমদেযলরমিল, পযযারলেএিাঅস্পষ্টরলয়পগলি।পজাসালররপ্রধান

যিেযেো, যারনািমিলইিলহালিে, োররাজারজনেএযমিলম্বা, আরওমেিাযষেযসিামধমনিোলের

েমরযেনাযলরমিললনএযমিরউেলরোথলররস্তূেগুললালযস্তুেযলর, ধীলরধীলরপসগুললালযপিাি

যলর, যাবেেিালনেমরমেেআযৃমেবেমরযলরপিেমেরামিিবেরীহয়।পজাসার১৯বিরধলররাজে

যলরমিললনবললিলনযরাহয়, েলবমযিুইমেহাসমবদএবংমিক্ষামবদোরমনমিে

স্মৃমেস্তলম্ভরসংখো

এবংআযালররযারেমহলসলবোরপবমিমদলনরিাসনলযদায়ীযরলিন।

C

The Step Pyramid has been thoroughly (েুঙ্খানুেুঙ্খভালব) examined (েরীক্ষাযরা) and

investigated (েদন্তযরা) over the last century, and it is now known that the building

process (প্রমক্রয়া) went through many different stages (েযোলয়). Historian Marc (িাযে) Van

(ভোন) de (রড) Mieroop (মিয়ালরাে) comments (িন্তবে) on this, writing ‘Much

Page 305 / 598

Page | 304

experimentation (েরীক্ষা-মনরীক্ষা) was involved (জমড়ে), which is especially clear in the

construction (মনিোে) of the pyramid in the center of the complex. It had several

plans … before it became the first Step Pyramid in history, piling six levels on top of

one another … The weight (ওজন) of the enormous (মবিাল) mass (ভর) was a challenge

for the builders (মনিোো), who placed the stones at an inward (অভেন্তরীে) incline (পঝাঁয) in

order to prevent (প্রমেলরাধ) the monument breaking up.’

পিেমেরামিিমিগেিোব্দীলেেুঙ্খানুেুঙ্খভালবেরীক্ষাযরাহলয়লিএবংেদন্তযরাহলয়লিএবং

এমিএখনজানাযায়পযমবমর্ল্ংপ্রমক্রয়ামিমবমভন্নেযোলয়েললপগলি।ইমেহাসমবদিাযেভোনমিমিয়ালরাে

এমবষলয়িন্তবেযলরলিন, মেমনমললখলিন: ‘অলনযেরীক্ষা-মনরীক্ষাজমড়েমিল, যামবলিষযলর

যিলপ্ল্লেরপযলেমেরামিিমনিোলেস্পষ্ট।এমিরপবিযলয়যমিেমরযেনামিল… এমিইমেহালসর

প্রথিধালেরমেরামিিহওয়ারআলগ, এলযঅেলররউেলরিয়মিস্তরস্থােনযলর… মবিালভলররওজন

মনিোোলদরজনেএযমিেোললঞ্জমিল, যারাোথরগুললালযপ্রমেলরাধযরারজনেএযমিঅভেন্তরীেপঝাঁয

পরলখমিল।'

D

When finally completed, the Step Pyramid raised (ওেলরউঠা) 62 meters high and was

the tallest structure (যাঠালিা) of its time. The complex in which it was built was the size

of a city in ancient Egypt and included (অন্তভুেক্তও) a temple (িমন্দর), courtyards (উঠান),

shrines (িাজার), and living quarters for the priests (েুলরামহে). It covered a region (এলাযা)

of 16 hectares and was surrounded (পবমষ্টে) by a wall (প্রােীর) 10.5 meters high. The wall

had 13 false doors cut into it with only one true entrance (প্রলবিেথ) cut into the south-

east corner; the entire wall was then ringed (পঘরাও) by a trench (েমরখা) 750 meters long

and 40 meters wide. The false doors and the trench were incorporated (অন্তভুেক্ত) into the

complex to discourage unwanted (অযামেে) visitors. If someone wished to enter, he or

she would have needed to know in advance how to find the location of the true opening

in the wall. Djoser was so proud of his accomplishment (সম্পাদন) that he broke the

tradition (ঐমেহে) of having only his own name on the monument and had Imhotep’s

name carved (পখাদাইযরা) on it as well.

মিলএবংএলেএযমিিমন্দর, উঠানএবংেুলরামহেলদরথাযারঘরঅন্তভুেক্তমিল।এমি১৬পহক্টর

লম্বাএবং৪০মিিারেওড়াএযমিেমরখামদলয়পঘরামিল।অযামেেদিেযলদরমনরুৎসামহেযরারজনে

মিথোদরজাএবংেমরখালযযিলপ্ল্লেঅন্তভুেক্তযরাহলয়মিল।যমদপযউপ্রলবিযরলেোয়, োহলল

োলযআলগপথলযইজানলেহলোপখালাপ্রােীলররআসলঅবস্থানমিযীভালবখুঁলজোওয়াযায়।পজাসার

স্মৃমেস্তলম্ভশুধুমনলজরনািইরালখনমনবরংএঐমেহেপভলেপফললইিলহালিলেরনািওএলেপখাদাই

মিললন।

E

The burial (সিামধ) chamber (যক্ষ) of the tomb (সিামধ), where the king’s body was laid

(অমধিাময়ে) to rest, was dug (খননযরা) beneath (মনলে) the base (িূল) of the pyramid

(মেরামিি), surrounded (োরোলি) by a vast (মবিাল) maze (পগালযধাঁধা) of long tunnels (সুড়ে)

that had rooms off them to discourage (মনরুৎসামহেযরা) robbers (িাযাে). One of the most

mysterious (রহসেিয়) discoveries (আমবষ্কারগুললা) found inside the pyramid was a large

number of stone (োথর) vessels (োে). Over 40,000 of these vessels, of various forms

and shapes (আযার/আযৃমের), were discovered in storerooms off the pyramid’s

underground (ভূগভেস্থ) passages. They are inscribed (পখাদাইযরা) with the names of rulers

(িাসয) from the First and Second Dynasties (রাজবংি) of Egypt and made from different

kinds of stone. There is no agreement among scholars (েমণ্ডে) and archaeologists

(প্রত্নোমেয) on why the vessels were placed in the tomb of Djoser or what they were

supposed to represent (প্রমেমনমধেযরা). The archaeologist Jean-Philippe (মজন-মফমলে)

Lauer (লাউয়ার), who excavated (খননযরা) most of the pyramid and complex, believes

they were originally stored and then give a ‘proper burial’ by Djoser in his pyramid to

honour his predecessors (েূবেসূমরলদর). There are other historians (ইমেহাসমবদ), however,

who claim (দামব) the vessels were dumped (পফলা) into the shafts (খাদ) as yet another

attempt to prevent (প্রমেহে) grave robbers from getting to the king’s burial (সিামধ)

chamber (যক্ষ).

সিামধরসিামধযক্ষ, পযখালনরাজারিৃেলদহলযিাময়েযরাহলয়মিলএিামেরামিলিরপগাড়ারনীলে

মনরুৎসামহেযরলো।মেরামিলিরমভেলরোওয়াসবলেলয়রহসেিয়আমবষ্কারগুললারিলধেএযমিমিল

জাহাজগুললারিলধে৪০০০০মিরওপবমিআমবষ্কৃেহলয়মিল।এগুললামিিলররপ্রথিএবংমিেীয়

জাহাজগুললাপজাসালররসিামধলেস্থােনযরাহলয়মিলবাোলদরপ্রমেমনমধেযরারযথামিলোমনলয়

েমণ্ডেএবংপ্রত্নোমেযলদরিলধেপযানওেুমক্তপনই।প্রত্নোমেযমজন-মফমলেলাউয়ার, মযমনপবমিরভাগ

মেরামিিএবংযিলপ্ল্েখননযলরমিললন, মবোসযলরনপযপসগুললািূলেসংরক্ষেযরাহলয়মিলএবং

োরেরপজাসারোরমেরামিলিোরেূবেসূমরলদরসম্মানজানালে'যথাযথসিামহে’ যলরন।অবিে

অনেমযিুইমেহাসমবদরলয়লিনযারাদামবযলরনপযোেগুললাখালদপফললপদওয়াহলয়মিললাযামযনা

যবরপোরলদর/িাযােলদররাজারসিামধযক্ষপথলযপ্রমেহেযরারউলদোগমিললা।

F

Unfortunately (দুভোগেবিে), all of the precaution (সেযো) and intricate (জমিল) design

(নযিা) of the underground (ভূগভেস্থ) network did not prevent ancient robbers (িাযাে)

from finding a way in. Djoser’s grave (যবর) goods (মজমনসেে), and even his body, were

stolen (েুমর) at some point in the past and all archaeologists (প্রত্নোমেয) found were a

small number of his valuables overlooked (নজলরেড়া) by the thieves (পোর). There was

enough left throughout the pyramid and its complex, however, to astonish and amaze

(মবমস্মে) the archaeologists who excavated (খননযরা) it.

দুভোগেবিে, ভূগভেস্থপনিওয়ালযেরসিস্তসেযোএবংজমিলনযিাপ্রােীনিাযােলদরএযমিেথ

খুঁলজপেলেবাধাপদয়মন।অেীলেপজাসালররযবলররমজমনসেেএিনমযোরপদহওপযালনাএযসিলয়

G

Egyptologist (মিিরমবদ) Miroslav (মিলরাোভ) Verner (ভানোর) writes, ‘Few monuments

(স্মৃমেস্তম্ভ) hold a place in human history as significant (োৎেযেূেে) as that of the Step

Pyramid in Saqqara (সাকারা) … It can be said without exaggeration (অমেরমঞ্জে) that this

pyramid complex constitutes (গঠনযরা) a milestone (িাইলফলয) in the evolution (মববেেন)

of monumental (স্মারয) stone architecture (স্থােেে) in Egypt and in the world as a whole.’

The future of work

According to a leading business consultancy, 3-14% of the global workforce will need

to switch to a different occupation within the next 10-15 years, and all workers will need

to adapt as their occupations evolve alongside increasingly capable machines.

industrial revolution brought people past subsistence agriculture, and the corporate

The White Horse of Uffington

উরিংিগ্রনিসাোকর্াড়া

প্রেমঅনুগ্রেে

The cutting of huge figures or ‘geoglyphs’ into the earth of English hillsides (পাহাগ্রেি

ঢালুগাত্র্) has taken place for more than 3,000 years. There are 56 hill figures scattered

(ছোগ্রনাবাছরেগ্রেপো) around England, with the vast majority on the chalk downlands

(চযসবএলাক্ােউন্মুিেগ্রক্িপাহােিগ্রেগ্রছ) of the country’s southern counties. The

figures include giants, horses, crosses and regimental badges. Although the majority of

these geoglyphs date within the last 300 years or so, there are one or two that are much

older.

ইংমলি(ইংলোলের) োহাড়গুললারোলুগালেরিামিপযলিমবিালপ্রমেযৃমেবা‘মজওলাইফস’ বেমরর

মবষয়মি৩০০০এরপবমিবিরধলরঘলিআসলি।ইংলোেজুলড়৫৬মিোহামড়প্রমেযৃমেিমড়লয়আলি

যমদওএসযলমজওলাইফলসরপবমিরভালগরইবয়সমবগে৩০০বিলররিলধেমযংবাপেিনই, আলরা

The most famous of these figures is perhaps also the most mysterious – the Uffington

White Horse in Oxfordshire. The White Horse has recently been re-dated and shown to

be even older than its previously assigned ancient pre-Roman Iron Age* date. More

controversial is the date of the enigmatic (রবভ্রারন্তক্ি) Long Man of Wilmington in

Sussex. While many historians are convinced the figure is prehistoric, others believe

that it was the work of an artistic monk from a nearby priory (মো) and was created

between the 11th and 15th centuries.

সন্তুষ্ট, অনেরামবোসযলরপযএমিযািাযামিএযিলঠরএযজনমিেীসাধুরযাজএবংএযাদিপথলয

েঞ্চদিিোব্দীরপভেরবেমরযরাহলয়মিললা।

The method of cutting these huge figures was simply to remove the overlying

(চক্াগ্রনারক্ছুিউপগ্রিথাক্া) grass to reveal the gleaming (জ্বলজ্বলক্িা) white chalk

below. However, the grass would soon grow over the geoglyph again unless it was

regularly cleaned or scoured (ঘগ্রষঘগ্রষপরিষ্কািক্িা) by a fairly large team of people.

One reason that the vast majority of hill figures have disappeared is that when the

traditions associated with the figures faded, people no longer bothered or remembered

to clear away the grass to expose the chalk outline. Furthermore, over hundreds of years

the outlines would sometimes change due to people not always cutting in exactly the

same place, thus creating a different shape to the original geoglyph. That fact that any

ancient hill figures survive at all in England today is testament (চশষইচ্ছাপত্র্) to the

strength and continuity of local customs and beliefs which, in one case at least, must

stretch back over millennia.

এসযলমবিালপ্রমেযৃমেযািারউোয়মিমিললাশুধুঘালসরউেমরআস্তরেলযসমরলয়মনলেরজ্বলজ্বলল

The Uffington White Horse is a unique, stylised representation of a horse consisting of

a long, sleek back, thin disjointed legs, a streaming tail, and a bird-like beaked head.

The elegant (মাস্তজবত) creature almost melts into the landscape. The horse is situated 2.5

km from Uffington village on a steep close to the Late Bronze Age* (c. 7th century

BCE) hillfort (রগরিদুগব) of Uffington Castle and below the Ridgeway, a long-distance

Neolithic** track.

উমফংিনসাদাপঘাড়ামিহলেএযমিঅননে, আযৃমেপ্রদালনরিাধেলিফুমিলয়পোলাএযমিপঘাড়ার

প্রমেেমবপযিারএযমিলম্বা, িসৃেপলািিমেঠ, মেযনঅসংযুক্তো-গুললা, এযমিপ্রবামহেহলেথাযা

পলজএবংএযমিোমখরিলোপোখািাথা।িামজে

এইসৃমষ্টমিভূদৃলিেরসালথপ্রায়গললমিলিযায়।

পঘাড়ামিউমফংিনিািপথলয২.৫মযমিদূলরপব্রাঞ্জযুলগরপিষমদযযারউমফংিনদুলগেরমগমরদুলগেরযালি

The Uffington Horse is also surrounded by Bronze Age burial mounds. It is not far from

the Bronze Age cemetery of Lambourn Seven Barrows, which consists of more than 30

well-preserved burial mounds (মাটিিরঢরব). The carving (চখ্াদাইক্িাচক্াগ্রনাস্তজরনস)

has been placed in such a way as to make it extremely difficult to see from close quarters

(খ্ুবক্াগ্রছচথগ্রক্চদখ্া), and like many geoglyphs is best appreciated from the air.

Nevertheless, there are certain areas of the Vale of the White Horse, the valley

containing and named after the enigmatic creature, from which an adequate impression

may be gained. Indeed on a clear day the carving can be seen from up to 30 km away.

উমফংিনপঘাড়ামিপব্রাঞ্জযুলগরসিামধমেমবিারাওেমরলবমষ্টে।এমিপব্রাঞ্জযুলগরলোিলবানেপসলভন

পবলরাসযবরস্থানপথলযদূলরনয়পযখালন৩০মিরওপবমিভাললাভালবসংরমক্ষেসিামধমেমবরলয়লি।

পখাদাইগুললাএিনভালবরাখাহলয়লিপযখুবযািপথলযপদখািাঅেেন্তযমঠনযরাহলয়লিএবংঅনোনে

মজওলাইলফরিলোবাোলসরিারাপসরািূলোয়নিাোয়।যমদওসাদাপঘাড়ারউেেেযারমনমদেষ্টমযিু

এলাযারলয়লি, উেেেযামিরহসেিয়সৃমষ্টলযধারেযরলিএবংএরপথলযইনািযরেযৃেহলয়লি, পযমির

িাধেলিযলথষ্টেমরিালেেমরমেমেহয়লোোওয়াসম্ভব।অবিেএযেমরষ্কারমদলনপখাদাইগুললা৩০মযমি

দূরপথলযপদখাসম্ভব।

The earliest evidence of a horse at Uffington is from the 1070s CE when ‘White Horse

Hill’ is mentioned in documents from the nearby Abbey of Abingdon, and the first

reference to the horse itself is soon after, in 1190 CE. However, the carving is believed

to date back much further than that. Due to the similarity of the Uffington White Horse

to the stylised depictions (রেত্র্ণ) of horses on 1st century BCE coins, it had been thought

that the creature must also date to that period.

উমফংিলনরপঘাড়ারসবলেলয়েুলরালনা/প্রথিমদযযারপ্রিাে/আলািেমি১০৭০মিিাব্দপথলযএলসলি

যখন‘পহায়াইিপহাসেমহল’-পযমনযিবেেীএলবঅবআমবংিলনরদমললামদলেউলেখযরাহলয়লিএবং

পখাদপঘাড়ামিরপ্রথিউলেখমিমঠযএরেরইোওয়াযায়, ১১৯০মিিাব্দপথলয।যমদওমবোসযরা

হয়পযপখাদাইগুললাএরওঅলনযআলগযার।মিিেূবেপ্রথিিেলযরযলয়লনরযারুযাযেিমণ্ডেপঘাড়ার

মেেরসলেউমফংিলনরসাদাপঘাড়ারমিলথাযায়এমিধারোযরাহলয়আসলিপযসৃমষ্টমিঅবিেইপসই

সিয়যাললরমদযযারইহলব।

However, in 1995 Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) testing was carried out by

the Oxford Archaeological Unit on soil from two of the lower layers of the horse’s body,

and from another cut near the base. The result was a date for the horse’s construction

somewhere between 1400 and 600 BCE – in other words, it had a Late Bronze Age or

Early Iron Age origin.

যমদও১৯৯৫সাললঅেলফািেনৃোমেযইউমনলিরিারাপঘাড়ামিরিরীলররমনলেরদুইস্তলররিামিএবং

মনলেরযািাযামিআলরযমিখনলনরিামিরওেরঅেমিযোমলমিমিউলললিিলুেমিমনলসন্সেরীক্ষা

েমরোমলেহয়।ফলাফললপযপঘাড়ারিরীলররপক্ষলেমনিোেযালযেরএিনএযমিসিয়যালমিললাযা

মযনা১৪০০এবং৬০০মিিেূলবেরিলধেহলব– অনেযথায়এমিরপব্রাঞ্জযুলগরপিষমদযযারবা

পল হযুলহরপ্রথিমদযযারসিলয়রউৎেমিস্থলরলয়লি।

The latter end of this date range would tie the carving of the horse in with occupation

of the nearby Uffington hillfort, indicating that it may represent a tribal emblem making

the land of the inhabitants of the hillfort. Alternatively, the carving may have been

carried out during a Bronze or Iron Age ritual. Some researchers see the horse as

representing the Celtic*** horse goddess Epona, who was worshipped as a protector of

horses, and for her associations with fertility. However, the cult of Epona was not

imported from Gaul (France) until around the first century CE. This date is at least six

centuries after the Uffington Horse was probably carved. Nevertheless, the horse had

great ritual and economic significance during the Bronze and Iron Ages, as attested by

its depictions on jewellery and other metal objects. It is possible that the carving

represents a goddess in native mythology, such as Rhiannon, described in later Welsh

mythology as a beautiful woman dressed in gold and riding a white horse.

এইসিয়যাললরপিলষরভাগমিহয়লোপঘাড়ারপখাদাইলযমনযিবেেীউমফংিনমগমরদুলগেরপেিারসালথ

সম্পমযে

Wendy Moore reviews Ed Yong’s book about microbes

ওগ্রেস্তেচমািঅণুজীবসম্পগ্রক্বএডইগ্রোংগ্রেিবইটিপযবাগ্রলােনাক্গ্রিগ্রছন

Microbes, most of them bacteria, have populated this planet since long before animal

life developed and they will outlive (ক্াগ্রিাচেগ্রেচবরশরদনচবঁগ্রেথাক্া) us. Invisible to

the naked eye, they are ubiquitous (সবববযাপী). They inhabit the soil, air, rocks and water

and are present within every form of life, from seaweed (সামুরিক্উস্তিদ) and coral to

dogs and humans. And, as Yong explains in his utterly absorbing (রেত্তাক্ষবক্) and

hugely important book we mess with them at our peril (িোবহরবপদ/রবপদচডগ্রক্

আনা).

Every species has its own colony of microbes, called a ‘microbiome’, and these

microbes vary not only between species but also between individuals and within

different parts of each individual. What is amazing is that while the number of human

cells in the average person is about 30 trillion, the number of microbial ones is higher

– about 39 trillion. At best, Yong informs us, we are only 50 per cent human. Indeed,

some scientists even suggest we should think of each species and its microbes as a single

unit, dubbed a ‘holobiont’.

ইউমনিমহলসলবপদখাউমেে, পযমিলযবলাহলে‘পহাললামবলয়ান্ট’।

In each human there are microbes that live only in the stomach, the mouth or the armpit

(বগল) and by and large (সারববক্িাগ্রব) they do so peacefully. So ‘bad’ microbes are just

microbes out of context. Microbes that sit contentedly (পরিতৃরপ্ত) in the human gut

(অি) (where there are more microbes than there are stars in the galaxy) can become

deadly if they find their way into the bloodstream. These communities are constantly

changing too. The right hand shares just one sixth of its microbes with the left hand.

And, of course, we are surrounded by microbes. Every time we eat, we swallow a

million microbes in each gram of food; we are continually swapping (রবরনমেক্িা)

microbes with other humans, pets and the world at large.

It’s a fascinating topic and Yong, a young British science journalist, is an extraordinarily

adept (চক্াগ্রনারবষগ্রেদারুণদক্ষ) guide. Writing with lightness and panache (বোই

িাব), he has a knack (দক্ষতা) of explaining complex science in terms that are both easy

to understand and totally enthralling (রবমুগ্ধক্িা). Yong is on a mission. Leading us

gently by the hand, he takes us into the world of microbes – a bizarre, alien planet – in

a bid to persuade us to love them as much as he does. By the end, we do.

উভয়মিই।ইয়ংএযমিিলনরলয়লিন।

For most of human history we had no idea that microbes existed. The first man to see

these extraordinarily potent creatures was a Dutch lens-maker called Antony van

Leeuwenhoek in the 1670s. Using microscopes of his own design that could magnify

up to 270 times, he examined a drop of water from a nearby lake and found it teeming

with tiny creatures he called ‘animalcules’. It wasn’t until nearly two hundred years

later that the research of French biologist Louis Pasteur indicated that some microbes

caused disease. It was Pasteur’s ‘germ theory’ that gave bacteria the poor image that

endures today.

Yong’s book is in many ways a plea (অনুগ্রিাি) for microbial tolerance, pointing out

that while fewer than one hundred species of bacteria bring disease, many thousands

more play a vital role in maintaining our health. The book also acknowledges that our

attitude towards bacteria is not a simple one. We tend to see the dangers posed by

bacteria, yet at the same time we are sold yoghurts and drinks that supposedly nurture

‘friendly’ bacteria. In reality, says Yong, bacteria should not be viewed as either friends

or foes, villains or heroes. Instead we should realise we have a symbiotic (রমগ্রথাজীবী)

relationship, that can be mutually beneficial or mutually destructive.

What then do these millions of organisms do? The answer is pretty much everything.

New research is now unravelling the ways in which bacteria aid digestion, regulate our

immune systems, eliminate toxins, produce vitamins, affect our behaviour and even

combat obesity. ‘They actually help us become who we are,’ says Yong. But we are

facing a growing problem. Our obsession (বদ্ধসংস্কাি, চঘাি, আগ্রবশ) with hygiene, our

overuse of antibiotics and our unhealthy, low-fibre diets are disrupting the bacterial

balance and may be responsible for soaring rates of allergies and immune problems,

such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

The most recent research actually turns accepted norms (আদশব/মানদণ্ড) upside down.

For example, there are studies indicating that the excessive use of household detergents

and antibacterial products actually destroys the microbes that normally keep the more

dangerous germs at bay. Other studies show that keeping a dog as a pet gives children

early exposure (অনাবৃতক্িণ) to a diverse range of bacteria, which may help protect

them against allergies later.

The readers of Yong’s book must be prepared for a decidedly unglamorous world.

Among the less appealing case studies is one about a fungus that is wiping out entire

populations of frogs and that can be halted (থামাগ্রনা) by a rare microbial bacterium.

Another is about squid that carry luminescent bacteria that protect them against

predators. However, if you can overcome your distaste for some of the investigations,

the reasons for Yong’s enthusiasm become clear. The microbial world is a place of

wonder. Already, in an attempt to stop mosquitoes spreading dengue fever – a disease

that infects 400 million people a year – mosquitoes are being loaded with a bacterium

to block the disease. In the future, our ability to manipulate microbes means we could

construct buildings with useful microbes built into their walls to fight off infections.

Just imagine a neonatal (নবজাতক্-সংক্রান্ত) hospital ward coated in a specially mixed

cocktail of microbes so that babies get the best start in life.

How to make wise decisions

যীভালবমবেক্ষেলদরিলোমসিান্তমনলেহয়

Across cultures, wisdom (রবেক্ষণতা) has been considered one of the most revered

(গিীিশ্রদ্ধাক্িা) human qualities. Although the truly wise may seem few and far

between (রবিল), empirical research examining wisdom suggests that it isn’t an

exceptional trait (তবরশষ্টয) possessed by a small handful of bearded philosophers after

all – in fact, the latest studies suggest that most of us have the ability to make wise

decisions, given the right context.

‘It appears that experiential, situational, and cultural factors are even more powerful in

shaping wisdom than previously imagined,’ says Associate Professor Igor Grossmann

of the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada. ‘Recent empirical findings from

cognitive,

social,

and

psychology

across experiential and situational contexts. Understanding the role of such contextual

factors offers unique insights into understanding wisdom in daily life, as well as how it

can be enhanced and taught.’

It seems that it’s not so much that some people simply possess wisdom and others lack

it, but that our ability to reason wisely depends on a variety of external factors. ‘It is

impossible to characterize thought processes attributed to wisdom without considering

the role of contextual factors,’ explains Grossmann. ‘In other words, wisdom is not

solely an “inner quality” but rather unfolds as a function of situations people happen to

be in. Some situations are more likely to promote wisdom than others.’

Coming up with a definition of wisdom is challenging, but Grossmann and his

colleagues have identified four key characteristics as part of a framework of wise

reasoning. One is intellectual humility or recognition of the limits of our own

knowledge, and another is appreciation of perspectives wider than the issue at hand.

Sensitivity to the possibility of change in social relations is also key, along with

compromise or integration of different attitudes and beliefs.

Grossmann and his colleagues have also found that one of the most reliable ways to

support wisdom in our own day-to-day decisions is to look at scenarios from a third-

party perspective, as though giving advice to a friend. Research suggests that when

adopting a first-person viewpoint we focus on ‘the focal features of the environment’

and when we adopt a third-person, ‘observer’ viewpoint we reason more broadly and

focus more on interpersonal and moral ideals such as justice and impartiality. Looking

at problems from this more expansive viewpoint appears to foster cognitive processes

related to wise decisions.

What are we to do, then, when confronted with situations like a disagreement with a

spouse or negotiating a contract at work, that require us to take a personal stake?

Grossmann argues that even when we aren’t able to change the situation, we can still

evaluate these experiences from different perspectives.

For example, in one experiment that took place during the peak of a recent economic

recession, graduating college seniors were asked to reflect on their job prospects. The

students were instructed to imagine their career either ‘as if you were a distant observer’

or ‘before your own eyes as if you were right there’. Participants in the group assigned

to the ‘distant observer’ role displayed more wisdom-related reasoning (intellectual

humility and recognition of change) than did participants in the control group.

In another study, couples in long-term romantic relationships were instructed to

visualize an unresolved relationship conflict either through the eyes of an outsider or

from their own perspective. Participants then discussed the incident with their partner

Page 326 / 598

Page | 325

for 10 minutes, after which they wrote down their thoughts about it. Couples in the

‘other’s eyes’ condition were significantly more likely to rely on wise reasoning –

recognizing others’ perspectives and searching for a compromise – compared to the

couples in the egocentric condition.

‘Ego-decentering promotes greater focus on others and enables a bigger picture,

conceptual view of the experience, affording recognition of intellectual humility and

change,’ says Grossmann.

We might associate wisdom with intelligence or particular personality traits, but

research shows only a small positive relationship between wise thinking and crystallized

intelligence and the personality traits of openness and agreeableness. ‘It is remarkable

how much people can vary in their wisdom from one situation to the next, and how much

stronger such contextual effects are for understanding the relationship between wise

judgment and its social and affective outcomes as compared to the generalized “traits”,’

Grossmann explains. ‘That is, knowing how wisely a person behaves in a given situation

is more informative for understanding their emotions or likelihood to forgive [or]

retaliate as compared to knowing whether the person may be wise “in general”.’

Cambridge-16, Test-3, Passage-1

Roman shipbuilding and navigation

কিামানগ্রেিজাহাজরনমঘাণএবংকন চালনরবেযা

Shipbuilding today is based on science and ships are built using computers and

sophisticated tools. Shipbuilding in ancient Rome, however, was more of an art relying

on estimation, inherited techniques and personal experience. The Romans were not

traditionally sailors but mostly land-based people, who learned to build ships from the

people that they conquered, namely (যথা, অথোৎ) the Greeks and the Egyptians.

আজজাহাজমনিোলেরমবষয়মিমবজ্ঞালনরওেরমভমিযলরেমরোমলেহয়এবংজাহাজগুললালয

যমম্পউিারওজমিলসরঞ্জািবেবহারযলরমনিোেযরাহয়।যমদওপ্রােীনপরালিপ্রােীনপরালিজাহাজ

মনিোেমিললাঅলনযিামিলেরিলো, যাঅনুিান, েূবেুরুষলদরপথলযপ্রাপ্তপয িলওবেমক্তগে

অমভজ্ঞোরওেরমনভেরযরলো।পরািনরাঐমেহামসযভালবনামবযমিললননাবরংঅমধযাংিপক্ষলেই

ভূমি-মভমিযিানুষমিললন, যারাজাহাজমনিোেযরািাপসসবিানুষলদরপথলযমিলখমিললনযালদরোরা

জয়যলরমিললন, অথোৎমিযএবংমিিরীয়লদরপথলয।

There are a few surviving written documents that give descriptions and representations

(রূোয়ন) of ancient Roman ships, including the sails and rigging (োলিারাসজ্জমে

যরা/োললযধলররাখাদমড়, জোযপ্রভৃমেরসিমষ্ট). Excavated (খননযৃে, এখালনোমনরমনেপথলয

উিারযৃে) vessels also provide some clues about ancient shipbuilding techniques. Studies

of these have taught us that ancient Roman shipbuilders built the outer hull (জাহালজর

যাঠালিা) first, then proceeded with the frame and the rest of the ship. Planks (েক্তা) used

to build the outer hull were initially sewn (পসলাইযলরপজাড়াপদওয়া) together. Starting

from the 6th century BCE, they were fixed using a method called mortise (যালঠরিুযলরার

মযনারায়খাঁজযািারিাধেলিঅনেআলরযমিসিজােীয়িুযলরারিাধেলিপসমিলযপজাড়াপদওয়া) and

tenon (খাঁলজরিলধেপোযালনাযায়এিনযলরোঁিাযালঠরপ্রান্তভাগ), whereby (যারসাহালযে) one

plank (েক্তা) locked into another without the need for stitching. Then in the first centuries

of the current era, Mediterranean

(ভূিধেসাগরীয়) shipbuilders shifted to another

shipbuilding method, still in use today, which consisted of building the frame (যাঠালিা,

যঙ্কাল) first and then proceeding with the hull and the other components of the ship. This

method was more systematic and dramatically shortened ship construction times. The

ancient Romans built large merchant ships and warships whose size and technology

were unequalled until the 16th century CE.

এখলনামযিুঅবমিষ্টমলমখেনমথরলয়লিপযগুললাপ্রােীনপরািানজাহাজগুললারবোোলরবেেনাও

পসগুললাররূোয়নযলর, যারিধেরলয়লিোলএবংপসমিলযধলররাখারমিওঅনোনেযাঠালিারসিমষ্ট।

োমনরেললদিহলেউিারযৃেজাহাজগুললাওপ্রােীনজাহাজমনিোেপয িলসিূহসম্পলযেমযিুসূে

প্রদানযলর।মিিেূবে৬ষ্ঠিেযপথলযএগুললািরমিসএেপিলনান(খাঁজযািাএবংপসইখাঁলজঅনে

আলরযমিিুযলরাপজাড়ালাগালনা) নালিরএযেিমেরিাধেলিমঠযযরাহলোপযখালনএযমিযালঠর

িুযলরাআলরযমিরসালথপযালনাপসলাইলয়রপ্রলয়াজনিাড়াইআবিহলয়পযলো।এরেরবেেিানযুলগর

প্রথিিোব্দীপথলযভূিধেসাগরীয়জাহাজমনিোোরাআলরযমিজাহাজমনিোেেিমেলেসলরযান, পযমি

আজওবেবহৃেহয়, যারিলধেরলয়লিযঙ্কালমিলযপ্রথলিমনিোেযরাএবংেলরজাহালজরিূলযাঠালিা

এবংঅনোনেঅংলিরমদলযধামবেহওয়া।এইেিমেমিআলরামনয়িিামফযমিললাএবংনািযীয়ভালব

জাহাজমনিোলেরসিয়লযযমিলয়এলনমিললা।প্রােীনপরািয়ানরাবৃহৎবামেজেজাহাজএবংযুিজাহাজ

মনিোেযরলোপযগুললারআযারএবংপ্রযুমক্ত১৬িিেযেযেন্তঅসািানেমিললা।

Warships were built to be lightweight and very speedy. They had to be able to sail near

the coast which is why they had no ballast (জাহাজলযমস্থররাখারজনেোরেললদলিস্থামেে

ভামরদ্রবামদ) or excess load and were built with a long, narrow hull. They did not sink

when damaged and often would lie crippled (অেমবহীন) on the sea’s surface following

Page 328 / 598

Page | 327

naval battles. They had a bronze battering ram (আঘােয), which was used to pierce (মিদ্র

যরা) the timber (যাঠ) hulls or break the oars (ববঠা) of enemy vessels. Warships used both

wind (sails) and human power (oarsmen) and were therefore very fast. Eventually,

Rome’s navy became the largest and most powerful in the Mediterranean, and the

Romans had control over what they therefore called Mare Nostrum meaning ‘our sea’.

যুিজাহাজগুললালযহাল্কাওজলনরএবংঅেেন্তদ্রুেগমেসম্পন্নযলরমনিোেযরলেহলো।োলদরলয

উেযূললরমনযিবেেীএলাযায়ভাসারউেলযাগীহলেহলোপযযারলেপসগুললারেললদলিপযালনাভামর

বস্তুবাঅমেমরক্তপবাঝাথাযলোনাএবংএযমিলম্বাওসংযীেেযাঠালিািারামনিোেযরাহলো।এগুললা

ক্ষমেিস্তহললিুলবপযলোনাএবংঅলনযসিয়পন যুলিরেরঅেমবহীনভালবসিুদ্রেৃলষ্ঠশুলয়থাযলো।

এগুললারএযমিপব্রালঞ্জরআঘােযমিললাপযমিলযিত্রুজাহালজরযালঠরযাঠালিালযমিদ্রযলরালেএবং

ববঠাগুললালযপভলেমদলেবেবহারযরাহলো।যুিজাহাজগুললাবাোস(োল) এবংিানবিমক্ত

(ববঠাোলয) উভলয়রইবেবহারযরলোএবংপযযারলেঅেেন্তদ্রুেগমেসম্পন্নমিললা।েমরোলি, পরালির

পন বামহনীভূিধেসাগলরবৃহিিএবংসবলেলয়িমক্তিালীপন বামহনীলেেমরেেহয়এবংপরািানলদরহালে

পসসিস্তজায়গায়মনয়িেমিললাপযগুললালযোরাফলশ্রুমেলেবললোিালরনস্ট্রুিযারঅথেদাঁড়ায়

আিালদরসাগর।

There were many kinds of warship. The ‘trireme’ was the dominant warship from the

7th to 4th century BCE. It had rowers (ববঠাোলয) in the top, middle and lower levels, and

approximately 50 rowers in each bank (প্রােীনমিিওপরািজাহাজগুললারদাঁমড়/ববঠাোলযলদর

আসনেংমক্ত). The rowers at the bottom had the most uncomfortable position as they were

under the other rowers and were exposed to the water entering through the oar-holes. It

is worth noting that contrary to popular perception, rowers were not slaves but mostly

Roman citizens enrolled in the military. The trireme was superseded (স্থলামভমষক্তহওয়া)

by larger ships with even more rowers.

পসসিয়অলনযধরলনরযুিজাহাজমিললা।‘মট্রলরলি’ মিিেূবে৭িপথলয৪থেিেযঅবমধএযমি

প্রভাবিালীজাহাজমিললা।এমিরউেলরর, িালঝরএবংমনলেরেলাগুললায়ববঠাোললযরামনলয়ামজে

থাযলেনএবংপ্রলেেযআসনেংমক্তলেআনুিামনয৫০জনযলরববঠাোলযথাযলেন।োলামনলেথাযা

ববঠাোললযরসবলেলয়অস্বমস্তযরঅবস্থানমিললাপযলহেুোরাঅনোনেববঠাোললযরমনলেথাযলেনএবং

ববঠারগলেেরপভেরমদলয়আসাোমনপথলযঅরমক্ষেঅবস্থায়থাযলে।এমিউলেখলযাগেমবষয়পয

জনমপ্রয়ধারোরমবেরীলেববঠাোলযরাদাসনয়বরংপবমিরভাগপক্ষলেইসািমরযবামহনীলেমনযুক্ত

পরািাননাগমরযরাহলেন।‘মট্রলরলি’ েলরআলরাবড়জাহাজিারাপ্রমেস্থামেেহয়পযখালনআলরাপবমি

দাঁমড়মিললন।

Page 329 / 598

Page | 328

Merchant ships were built to transport lots of cargo over long distances and at a

reasonable cost. They had a wider hull, double planking (েক্তামদলয়োযা) and a solid

interior for added stability. Unlike warships, their V-shaped hull was deep underwater,

meaning that they could not sail too close to the coast. They usually had two huge side

rudders (জাহালজরহাল), located off the stern (জাহালজরেিােভাগ) and controlled by a small

tiller (জাহালজরহালপঘারালনারহােল) bar connected to a system of cables. They had from

one to three masts (িাস্তুল) with large square sails and a small triangular sail at the bow

(বক্রভাগ). Just like warships, merchant ships used oarsmen, but coordinating the

hundreds of rowers in both types of ship was not an easy task. In order to assist them,

music would be played on an instrument, and oars would then keep time with this.

বামেজেজাহাজগুললাঅলনযেমরিালেিালািালএযমিনোযেখরলেঅলনযদূরবেেীজায়গায়েমরবহন

যরারজনেমনিোেযরাহলো।পসগুললারমবস্তৃেযাঠালিা, েক্তারমিস্তরএবংএযমিবমলষ্ঠঅন্তভোগমিললা

যালেযলরপবমিস্থাময়েপদওয়াযায়।যুিজাহাজগুললারমবেরীলেএগুললার‘V’-আযৃমেরযাঠালিাোমনর

গভীলরেললপযলো, যারঅথেহলেএগুললাউেযূললরখুবযালিভাসলেোরলোনা।এগুললারসাধারেে

দুইমিমবিালোেেহালমিললাপযগুললাজাহালজরেিােভালগরযালিমিললাএবংএগুললাএযমিযোবল

মসলিলিসংযুক্তএযমিপিািহােলিারামনয়মিেহলো।পসগুললারমবিালবগোযৃমেরোললরসালথ

এযমিপথলযমেনমিিাস্তুলথাযলোএবংজাহালজরবক্রভালগআলরযমিপিািমেভুজাযৃমেরোল

থাযলো।যুিজাহাজলদরিলোইবামেজেজাহাজগুললাওববঠাোলযবেবহারযরলোমযন্তুউভয়ধরলনর

জাহালজইযলয়যলিাববঠাোলযলদরিালঝসিিয়সাধনযরাপযালনাসহজযাজমিললানা।োলদরলয

সহায়োযরােজনেএযমিবাদেযিমদলয়সুরবাজালেহলোএবংববঠাগুললােখনপসইসুলররসিলয়র

সালথোলমিমললয়েললেোরলো।

The cargo on merchant ships included raw materials (e.g. iron bars, copper, marble and

granite), and agricultural products (e.g. grain from Egypt’s Nile valley). During the

Empire, Rome was a huge city by ancient standards of about one million inhabitants.

Goods from all over the world would come to the city through the port of Pozzuoli

situated west of the bay of Naples in Italy and through the gigantic port of Ostia situated

at the mouth of the Tiber River. Large merchant ships would approach the destination

port and, just like today, be intercepted by a number of towboats (অনেপন যালযপযপন যা

পিলনআলন) that would drag them to the quay.

বামেজেজাহাজগুললারিালািাললরিলধেমিললািক্তউোদান(পযিন– পলাহারবার, যোর, িালবেলএবং

িানাইি) এবংযৃমষজেেে(পযিন- মিিলররমনলউেেেযারিসে)।সম্রালজেরসিয়পরািপ্রােীন

আদিেিানঅনুসালরদিলক্ষবসবাসযারীরএযমিমবিালিহরমিললা।মবলেরসযলস্থানপথলয

Page 330 / 598

Page | 329

িালািালপনেলসউেসাগলররেমিলিঅবমস্থেইোমলরপোলজ্জামলবন্দরএবংমিবারনদীরিুলখ

অবমস্থেদানবাযৃমেরঅমিয়াবন্দলররিাধেলিহয়লোিহরমিলেআসলো।মবিালবামেজেজাহাজগুললা

হয়লোআজলযরিলোইযামঙ্ক্ষেবন্দলররমদলযধামবেহলো, পযখালনমনমদেষ্টসংখেযপিালবালিরিাধেলি

পসগুললারেথলরাধহলয়আসলোপযগুললাোলদরপজমিঘািেযেন্তপিলনমনলয়পযলো।

The time of travel along the many sailing routes could vary widely. Navigation in

ancient Rome did not rely on sophisticated instruments such as compasses but on

experience, local knowledge and observation of natural phenomena. In conditions of

good visibility, seamen in the Mediterranean often had the mainland or islands in sight,

which greatly facilitated navigation. They sailed by noting their position relative to a

succession (অনুক্রি) of recognisable landmarks. When weather conditions were not good

or where land was no longer visible, Roman mariners estimated directions from the pole

star (ধ্রুবোরা) or, with less accuracy, from the Sun at noon. They also estimated

directions relative to the wind and swell (ঝলড়রেরসাগলররজলরামিরধীরউত্থান-েেন,

েরেমবলক্ষাভ) . Overall, shipping in ancient Roman times resembled (মিলখাওয়া) shipping

today with large vessels regularly crossing the seas and bringing supplies from their

Empire.

অলনযগুললাজাহাজেলাররুলিভ্রিলেরসিয়মবস্তরভালবমভন্নমভন্নহলেোলর।প্রােীনপরালিপন োলনা

জমিলযিোমেপযিনযম্পালসরওেরমনভেরযরলোনাবরংঅমভজ্ঞো, স্থানীয়জ্ঞানএবংপ্রাযৃমেয

ঘিনারেযোললােনারওেরমনভেরযরলো।ভাললাদৃিেিানোরিলোেমরমস্থমেলেভূিধেসাগলরনামবয

অলনযসিয়িূলভূখণ্ডমযংবািীেেুঞ্জলযদৃমষ্টসীিারিলধেপেলেন, যাপন োলনায়দারুেভালবসাহাযে

যরলো।োরাপেনাযায়এিনপভ গমলযসীিানারঅনুক্রিঅনুসালরমনলজলদরঅবস্থানমেমিেযলর

যাোশুরুযরলো।যখনআবহাওয়ারেমরমস্থমেভাললাথাযলোনামযংবাপযখালনস্থলভাগআরপদখা

পযলোনা, পরািাননামবযরাধ্রুবোরারিাধেলিমযংবাআলরাযিমনভুেলোরসালথদুেুলরসূলযেরিাধেলি

গমেেথঅনুিানযরলো।োরাবায়ুপ্রবাহএবংেরেমবলক্ষালভরসালথসম্পযেযুক্তযলরওগমেেথ

জলবায়ুিপরিবেঘগ্রনিিগ্রলকবরিগ্রয়আসগ্রছনিওগ্রয়িেুষ্ািগ্ররাগ্রেিকিেগ্রিোকা

(এইপযাগ্রসগ্রজপিবেীগ্রেেীর্ঘসূত্রোএড়াগ্রনািজনযআিঘইগ্রিক্টশব্দটিগ্রকএিাগ্রবকলখাহগ্রব)

A

Well above the treeline (সিুদ্রেৃষ্ঠহলেপযউচ্চোয়মযংবাউিরওদমক্ষেমবষুবলরখারপযদূরবেেী

এলাযায়পযালনাগািজোয়না) in Norway’s highest mountains, ancient fields (এখালনউেুক্ত

প্রােন) of ice are shrinking as Earth’s climate warms. As the ice has vanished, it has been

giving up the treasures it has preserved in cold storage for the last 6,000 years – items

such as ancient arrows and skis from Viking Age* traders. And those artefacts have

provided archaeologists with some surprising insights into how ancient Norwegians

made their livings.

েৃমথবীরজলবায়ুউষ্ণহওয়ারফললনরওলয়রসুউচ্চেবেিালায়উমিদপবঁলেথাযারজনে(নূেনেি)

প্রলয়াজনীয়উচ্চোরওঅলনযউেলরবরলফরপ্রােীনউেুক্তপ্রােনগুললাসংযুমেেহলয়আসলি।পযলহেু

বরফগালয়বহলয়পগলি, োইএমিপসসবগুপ্তধনলযপিলড়মদলেপযগুললালযএমিমহিাগালরগে৬,০০০

বিরযাবেসংরক্ষেযলরপরলখমিললা– এিনমযিুমজমনসযারিলধেরলয়লিভাইমযংবমেযলদরআিললর

প্রােীনেীরএবংমস্ক।আরপসসযলিানবমনমিে

বস্তুপ্রােীননরওলয়মজয়ানরাযীভালবোলদরজীমবযা

মনবোহযরলোপসসম্পলযেনৃেেমবদলদরমযিুমবস্ময়যরঅন্তমনেমহেেেপ্রদানযলরলি।

*Viking Age: a period of European history from around 700 CE to around 1050 CE

when Scandinavian Vikings migrated throughout Europe by means of trade and warfare

B

Organic materials like textiles and hides (এখালনেশুরোিড়া) are relatively rare finds at

archaeological sites. This is because unless they’re protected from the microorganisms

that cause decay, they tend no to last long. Extreme cold is one reliable way to keep

artefacts relatively fresh for a few thousand years, but once thawed out (বরফগললেুনরায়

োমনলেেমরেেহওয়া), these materials experience degradation (অধঃেেন) relatively

swiftly.

পদহযিসম্পমযে

উোদান/মজমনসগুললাপযিনযােড়লবানারউোদানএবংেশুেিেএসযলনৃোমেয

পক্ষেসিূলহঅলেক্ষাযৃেমবরলমবষয়।যারেএগুললাযমদেেনসৃমষ্টযারীঅেুজীবলদরপথলযসুরমক্ষে

নাথালয, োহললপবমিমদনমিলযনা।প্রেণ্ডঠাণ্ডাহলেিানবমনমিে

এসযলউোদানেুলনািূলযভালবোড়াোমড়অধঃেমেেহয়।

With climate change shrinking ice cover around the world, glacial archaeologists need

to race the clock (এিনএযেমরমস্থমেযখনপযালনামযিুখুবদ্রুেোরসালথযরাপ্রলয়াজন) to find

newly revealed artefacts, preserve them, and study them. If something fragile dries and

is windblown it might very soon be lost to science, or an arrow might be exposed and

then covered again by the next snow and remain well-preserved. The unpredictability

means that glacial archaeologists have to be systematic in their approach to fieldwork.

পযহেুজলবায়ুেমরবেেনমবেজুলড়বরলফরআোদনলযসংযুমেেযলরেলললি, েুষারলস্রােমবষয়য

নৃেেমবদলদরসাম্প্রমেযসিলয়উলোমেেপ্রােীনিানবমনমিে

বস্তুগুললালযখুঁলজপবরযরলে, সংরক্ষে

যরলেএবংগলবষোযরলেদ্রুেোরসালথযাজযরলেহলব।যমদভেুরমযিুশুমযলয়এবংপসখালন

যমদবায়ুপ্রবাহথালযোহললহয়লোদ্রুেইএমিমবজ্ঞালনরযািপথলযহামরলয়যালবঅথবাএযমিেীর

হয়লোবাউেুক্তহলয়েড়লবএবংেলরআবালরাআলরযমিবরফিারাআোমদেহলয়েড়লবএবং

ভাললািলোসুরমক্ষেথাযলব।এইঅমনিয়োরঅথেহলেেুষারলস্রােমবষয়যনৃেেমবদলদরোলদরিাঠ

েযোলয়রউলদোলগমনয়ািানুগহলেহলব।

C

Over a nine-year period, a team of archaeologists, which included Lars Pilø of Oppland

County Council, Norway, and James Barrett of the McDonald Institute for

Archaeological Research, surveyed patches of ice in Oppland, an area of south-central

Norway that is home to some of the country’s highest mountains. Reindeer (বল্গাহমরে)

once congregated (জলড়াযরা/হওয়া) on these ice patches in the later summer months to

escape biting insects, and from the late Stone Age**, hunters followed. In addition,

trade routes threaded through (েথখুঁলজেলা) the mountain passes of Oppland, linking

settlements in Norway to the rest of Europe.

নয়বিলররএযমিসিয়যালবোেীনৃোমেযলদরএযমিদল, পযখালননরওলয়রঅেলোেযাউমন্ট

যাউমন্সললরলাসেমেললাএবংিোযলিানার্ল্ইনমিমিউিফরআমযেওলমজযোলমরসালেেরপজিসবোলরি

মিললন, পসইদলমিঅেলোলেবরলফরপবিমযিুিুযলরারওেরসিীক্ষাোলান, এমিদমক্ষে-িূলনরওলয়র

এযমিএলাযাপযমিপদিমিরউচ্চেরেবেিালারিলধেযলয়যমিরআবাসস্থল।এযসিয়এসববরফ

িুযলরায়/বরলফআোমদেজমিলেিীলেরপিষিাসগুললায়বল্গাহমরলেরএযমেেহলয়মিললাযালেযলর

এরাযািমড়লয়ধলরএিনপোযািাযড়, মিযামরএবংোথরযুলগরপিষমদযিাপথলযরক্ষাপেলেোলর।

The slow but steady movement of glaciers tends to destroy anything at their bases, so

the team focused on stationary (মনিল) patches of ice, mostly above 1,400 metres. That

ice is found amid fields of frost-weathered boulders (িসৃেপগালাযারমিলাখণ্ড), fallen rocks,

and exposed bedrock that for nine months of the year is buried beneath snow.

েুষারলস্রালেরধীরমযন্তুমনয়মিেসঞ্চালনএগুললারমনম্নাংলিথাযাপযলযালনামযিুধ্বংসযলরপফললোই

এইদলমিবরলফরমনিলিুযলরাগুললারওেরিলনামনলবিযলরলি, পযগুললারপবমিরভাগ১,৪০০

মিিালররওওেলর।এইবরফগুললামহিালঙ্করমনলেরআবহাওয়ায়থাযািসৃেপগালাযারমিলাখণ্ড, েমেে

োথলরএবংউেুক্তিক্তমিলারপ্রান্তলররিলধেোওয়াযায়পযগুললাবিলররনয়িাসবরলফরমনলেোো

থালয।

‘Fieldwork is hard work – hiking with all our equipment, often camping on permafrost

– but very rewarding. You’re rescuing the archaeology, bringing the melting ice to wider

attention, discovering a unique environmental history and really connecting with the

natural environment,’ says Barrett.

‘িাঠেযোলয়রযাজহলেযমঠনযাজ– আিালদরসযলসরঞ্জািমনলয়ভ্রিলেযাওয়া, অলনযসিয়ভূগভেস্থ

মেরমহিাময়েঅঞ্চললোঁবুিামেলয়থাযা– মযন্তুপবিফলপ্রসূ।আেমননৃোমেযমবষয়সিয়উিার

যরলিন, বরফগলারমবষয়মিবৃহিরিলনালযালগরআওোয়আনলিন, এযমিঅননেেমরলবিগেইমেহাস

উিারযরলিনএবংসমেেইপ্রাযৃমেযেমরলবলিরসালথসংযুক্তহলেন,’ বোলরিবলললিন।

**The Stone Age: a period in early history that began about 3.4 million years ago

D

At the edges of the contracting (সংযুমেে) ice patches, archaeologists found more than

2,000 artefacts, which formed a material record that ran from 4,000 BCE to the

beginnings of the Renaissance (১৪িিোব্দীরনবজেপথলয১৬িিোব্দীেযেন্তইউলরালেমিে

ওসামহলেেরেুনভুেদয়) in the 14th century. Many of the artefacts are associated with

hunting. Hunters would have easily misplaced arrows and they often discarded broken

bows rather than take them all the way home. Other items could have been used by

hunters traversing the high mountain passes of Oppland: all-purpose items like tools,

skis, and horse tack.

সংযুমেেবরফিুযলরাগুললারপযাোগুললায়নৃোমেযরা২০০০এরপবমিপ্রােীনিানবমনমিে

বস্তু

পেলয়লিনপযমিএযমিউোদালনরপরযিেবেমরযলরলিপযমিএযমিবস্তুগেপরযিেবেমরযলরলিপযমি

৪০০০মিিেূবেপথলয১৪িিেলযরপরলনঁসাসমবপ্ল্লবরশুরুেযেন্তমবস্তৃে।এসযলআিেইলফলক্টর

অলনযগুললামিযালররসালথসম্পমযে।মিযামররাহয়লোসহলজইেীলররফলালযস্থানেুেেযলর

পফললোএবংোরাঅলনযসিয়ভাোধনুযগুললালযবামড়েযেন্তমনলয়যাওয়ারবদললপফললমদলো।

অেলোলেরউঁেুোহাড়পঘঁষারাস্তাগুললায়ভ্রিেরেমিযামরলদরিারাবেবহৃেসবধরলনরযালজবেবহৃে

মজমনসপযিন– যিাংি, মস্কএবংপঘাড়ারনাল।

E

Barrett’s team radiocarbon-dated 153 of the artefacts and compared those dates to the

timing of major environmental changes in the region – such as periods of cooling or

warming – and major social and economic shifts – such as the growth of farming

settlements and the spread of international trade networks leading up (পযালনাএযঘিনার

েরপথলযঅনেআলরযমিমনমদেষ্টঘিনারআগেযেন্তসিয়) to the Viking Age. They found that

some periods had produced lots of artefacts, which indicates that people had been pretty

active in the mountains during those times. But there were few or no signs of activity

during other periods.

বোলরলিরদল১৫৩মিআিেইলফলক্টরপরমিওযাবেনলিমিংযলরলিনএবংপসসবোমরখলযপসইঅঞ্চললর

গুরুেেূেেেমরলবিগেেমরবেেলনরসিলয়রসালথেুলনাযলরলিন– পযিনিীেলবাউষ্ণায়লনর

সিয়যালএবংপ্রধানসািামজযওঅথেননমেযেমরবেেন– পযিনযৃমষজউেমনলবলিরউত্থানএবং

ভাইমযংলদরসিলয়রআগেযেন্তআন্তজোমেযবামেজেপনিওয়ালযেরমবস্তার।োরাখুঁলজোনপযমযিুমযিু

সিয়যালঅলনযগুললাআিেইলফক্টবেমরযলরলিপযমিইমেেপদয়পযপসসিয়গুললায়িানুষোহালড়পবি

সমক্রয়মিললা।মযন্তুঅনোনেসিয়যালগুললায়যাযেক্রলিরখুবযিবাপযালনামেিমিললানা।

F

What was surprising, according to Barrett, was the timing of these periods. Oppland’s

mountains present daunting (ভয়ঙ্কর) terrain (ভূখণ্ড) and in periods of extreme cold,

glaciers could block the higher mountain passes (মগমরেথ) and make travel in the upper

reaches of the mountains extremely difficult. Archaeologists assumed people would

stick to lower elevations during a time like the Late Antique Little Ice Age, a short

period of deeper-than-usual cold from about 536-600 CE. But it turned out that hunters

kept regularly venturing into (ঝুঁমযমনলয়পযালনাযাজযরা) the mountains even when the

climate turned cold, based on the amount of stuff they had apparently dropped there.

Many of the artefacts Barrett’s team recovered date from the beginning of the Viking

Age, the 700s through to the 900s CE. Trade networks connecting Scandinavia with

Europe and the Middle East were expanding around this time. Although we usually

think of ships when we think of Scandinavian expansion, these recent discoveries show

that plenty of goods travelled on overland routes, like the mountain passes of Oppland.

And growing Norwegian towns, along with export markets, would have created a

booming demand for hides to fight off the cold, as well as antlers (হমরলেরিাখামবভক্তমিং)

to make useful things like combs. Business must have been good for hunters.

H

Norway’s mountains are probably still hiding a lot of history – and prehistory –

in remote ice patches. When Barrett’s team looked at the dates for their sample

of 153 artefacts, they noticed a gap with almost no artefacts from about 3,800 to

2,200 BCE. In fact, archaeological finds from that period are rare all over Norway.

The researchers say that could be because many of those artefacts have already

disintegrated or are still frozen in the ice. That means archaeologists could be

extracting some of those artefacts from retreating ice in years to come.

An international team of scientists led by the University of Cambridge has discovered

that the ‘thermometer’ molecule (অেু) in plants enables (সক্ষিযরা/ক্ষিোপদওয়া) them to

develop according to seasonal temperature changes. Researchers have revealed that

molecules called phytochromes – used by plants to detect light during the day – actually

change their function in darkness to become cellular temperature gauges (িাোরযি) that

measure the heat of the night.

At night, these molecules change states, and the pace at which they change is ‘directly

stimulating (উদ্দীমেেযরা) plant growth.

Farmers and gardeners have known for hundreds of years how responsive plants are to

temperature: warm winters cause many trees and flowers to bud early, something

humans have long used to predict weather and harvest times for the coming year. The

latest research pinpoints (পযালনামযিুসম্পলযেএযদিসমঠযেথেআমবষ্কারবাবেেনাযরা) for the

first time a molecular mechanism in plants that reacts to temperature – often triggering

the buds of spring we long to see at the end of winter.

With weather and temperatures set to become ever more unpredictable due to climate

change, researchers say the discovery that this light-sensing molecule also functions as

the internal thermometer in plant cells could help us breed tougher crops. ‘It is estimated

that agricultural yields will need to double by 2050, but climate change is a major threat

to achieving this. Key crops such as wheat and rice are sensitive to high temperatures.

Thermal stress reduces crop yields by around 10% for every one degree increase in

temperature,’ says lead researcher Dr Philip Wigge from Cambridge’s Sainsbury

Laboratory. ‘Discovering the molecules that allow plants to sense temperature has the

potential to accelerate the breeding of crops resilient to thermal stress and climate

change.’

In their active state, phytochrome molecules bind themselves to DNA to restrict plant

growth. During the day, sunlight activates the molecules, slowing down growth. If a

plant finds itself in shade, phytochromes are quickly inactivated – enabling it to grow

faster to find sunlight again. This is how plants compete to escape each other’s shade.

‘Light-driven changes to phytochrome activity occur very fast, in less than a second,’

says Wigge.

সমক্রয়থাযাঅবস্থায়সাইলিালক্রািঅেুসিূহমনলজলদরমিএনএরসালথপবঁলধপফললযালেযলরউমিলদর

বধেনলযআিযালনাযায়।মদলনরপবলায়সূলযেরআললাঅেুগুললালযসমক্রয়যলরবধেনলযযমিলয়পদয়।

যমদপযালনাগািমনলজলযিায়ারিলধেআমবষ্কারযলর, সাইলিালক্রািগুললােখনদ্রুেসমক্রয়হলয়ওলঠ

– এমিলযদ্রুেবধেলনসক্ষিযলরপোললযালেপফরসূলযেরআললাপখাঁজাযায়।এভালবইউমিলদরাএলয

অেলররিায়াপথলযপবমরলয়আসলেপ্রমেলযাগীোযরা।‘সাইলিালক্রালিরযাযেক্রলিআললাযোমলে

েমরবেেনখুবদ্রুেসংঘমিেহয়, এযপসলযলেরওযিসিলয়,’ উইগবলললিন।

At night, however, it’s a different story. Instead of a rapid deactivation following

sundown, the molecules gradually change from their active to inactive state. This is

called ‘dark reversion (প্রেোবেেন)’. ‘Just as mercury rises in a thermometer, the rate at

which phytochromes revert to their inactive state during the night is a direct measure of

temperature,’ says Wigge.

যমদওরালেএমিএযমিমভন্নগে।সূযোলস্তরেরএযমিদ্রুেগমেরমনমিয়োরবদললঅেুগুললাধীলর

ধীলরসমক্রয়পথলযমনমিয়অবস্থায়েমরবমেে

হয়।এমিলয‘অন্ধযালরপ্রেোবেেন’ বলল।‘পযিনভালব

োরদথালিোমিিালরবৃমিোয়, রালেসাইলিালক্রািপযহালরমনমিয়অবস্থায়প্রেোবমেে

হলবপসমি

োেিাোরএযমিসরাসমরেমরিাে,’ উইগআলরাবললন।

F

‘The lower the temperature, the slower the rate at which phytochromes revert to

inactivity, so the molecules spend more time in their active, growth-suppressing state.

This is why plants are slower to grow in winter. Warm temperatures accelerate dark

reversion, so that phytochromes rapidly reach an inactive state and detach themselves

from the plant’s DNA – allowing genes to be expressed and plant growth to resume.’

Wigge believes phytochrome thermo-sensing evolved at a later stage, and co-opted the

biological network already used for light-based growth during the downtime of night.

G

Some plants mainly use day length as an indicator of the reason. Other species, such as

daffodils, have considerable temperature sensitivity, and can flower months in advance

during a warm winter. In fact, the discovery of the dual role of phytochromes provides

the science behind a well-known rhyme long used to predict the coming season: oak

before ash (এযধরলনরঅরলেেরবৃক্ষ) we’ll have a plash (োমনরঝােিা), ash before oak we’re

in for a soak (এলযবালরমভলজযাওয়া).

মযিুউমিদিূলেমদলনরবদঘেলযএইযারলেরএযমিসংলযেমহলসলববেবহারযলর।অনোনে

প্রজামেগুললাপযিনিোলফামিললরউলেখলযাগেোেিাোরপ্রমেসংলবদনিীলোরলয়লিএবংএযমিউষ্ণ

িীেযাললযলয়যিাসেূলবেইফুলমদলেোলর।এিনমযসাইলিালক্রালিরবিেভূমিযারআমবষ্কারেরবেেী

পি সুিসম্পলযেআনুিানযরারজনেদীঘেমদনধলরবেবহৃেএযমিঅমেেমরমেেিড়ারপেিলনরমবজ্ঞান

আিরাএলযবালরমভলজযাওয়ারঅলেক্ষায়।

Wigge explains: ‘Oak trees rely much more on temperature, likely using phytochromes

as thermometers to dictate development, whereas ash trees rely on measuring day length

to determine their seasonal timing. A warmer spring, and consequently a higher

likeliness of a hot summer, will result in oak leafing before ash. A cold spring will see

the opposite. As the British know only too well, a colder summer is likely to be a rain-

soaked one.’

উইগবোখোযলরন: ‘ওযগািোেিাোরওেরপবমিমনভেরযলর, সম্ভবেসাইলিালক্রািলযথালিোমিিার

মহলসলববেবহারযলরবধেনলযমনলদেিপদয়, পযখালনএিগািোলদরপি সুমিসিয়যালমনধোরলেমদলনর

বদঘেিাোরওেরমনভেরযলর।এযমিউষ্ণবসন্তএবংেরবেেীলেএযমিউষ্ণিীলেরঅমধযসম্ভাবনা

েমরোলিএলিরআলগওলযোোগজালব।এযমিিীেলবসন্তএরউলিািাপদখলব।পযলহেুপযবল

মব্রমিিরাইজালনপযএযমিিীেলিীেহয়লোবাএযমিবৃমষ্টলভজাহলব।

The new findings are the culmination (েূড়ান্ত) of twelve years of research involving

scientists from Germany, Argentina and the US, as well as the Cambridge team. The

work was done in a model system, using a mustard plant called Arabidopsis, but Wigge

says the phytochrome genes necessary for temperature sensing are found in crop plants

as well. ‘Recent advances in plant genetics now mean that scientists are able to rapidly

identify the genes controlling these processes in crop plants, and even alter their activity

using precise molecular “scalpels”(িলেিুমলযা),’ adds Wigge. ‘Cambridge is uniquely

well-positioned to do this kind of research as we have outstanding collaborators nearby

who work on more applied aspects of plant biology, and can help us transfer this new

knowledge into the field.’

An international team of scientists led by the University of Cambridge has discovered

that the ‘thermometer’ molecule (অেু) in plants enables (সক্ষিযরা/ক্ষিোপদওয়া) them to

develop according to seasonal temperature changes. Researchers have revealed that

change their function in darkness to become cellular temperature gauges (িাোরযি) that

measure the heat of the night.

যোিমব্রজমবেমবদোললয়রপনেৃলেমবজ্ঞানীলদরএযমিআন্তজোমেযদলআমবষ্কারযলরলিনপযউমিলদর

mercury in a thermometer. The warmer it is, the faster the molecular change –

stimulating (উদ্দীমেেযরা) plant growth.

Farmers and gardeners have known for hundreds of years how responsive plants are to

temperature: warm winters cause many trees and flowers to bud early, something

humans have long used to predict weather and harvest times for the coming year. The

latest research pinpoints (পযালনামযিুসম্পলযেএযদিসমঠযেথেআমবষ্কারবাবেেনাযরা) for the

first time a molecular mechanism in plants that reacts to temperature – often triggering

the buds of spring we long to see at the end of winter.

D

With weather and temperatures set to become ever more unpredictable due to climate

change, researchers say the discovery that this light-sensing molecule also functions as

the internal thermometer in plant cells could help us breed tougher crops. ‘It is estimated

that agricultural yields will need to double by 2050, but climate change is a major threat

to achieving this. Key crops such as wheat and rice are sensitive to high temperatures.

Thermal stress reduces crop yields by around 10% for every one degree increase in

temperature,’ says lead researcher Dr Philip Wigge from Cambridge’s Sainsbury

Laboratory. ‘Discovering the molecules that allow plants to sense temperature has the

potential to accelerate the breeding of crops resilient to thermal stress and climate

change.’

পযলহেুজলবায়ুেমরবেেলনরফললআবহাওয়াওোেিাোরসিমষ্টআলগপেলয়আলরাঅমনমিেহলয়

েড়লেেলললি, গলবষযরাবললনপযআললাযসংলবদীঅেুপযউমিদপযালষঅভেন্তরীেথালিোমিিার

মহলসলবওযাজযলরএইআমবষ্কারমিআিালদরআলরাদৃঢ়ফসললরফললনরসাহাযেযরলেোলর।‘এমি

প্রেোিাযরাহলেপযযৃমষজফলনলয২০৫০সালনাগাদমিগুেযরাপ্রলয়াজনহলব, মযন্তুএমিঅজেলনর

পক্ষলেজলবায়ুেমরবেেনএযমিবড়হুিময।গিএবংোললরিলোপ্রধানফসলগুললাউচ্চোেিাোর

প্রমেসংলবদনিীল।োেিাোরোেোেিাোয়প্রমে১মিমিরবৃমিলেফসললরফলনলয১০% এর

িলোযমিলয়আলন,’ এিনিাইবলললিনযোিমব্রলজরপসইনসবুমরগলবষোগালররিীষেগলবষযিক্টর

মফমলেওলয়জ।‘উমিদলদরোেিাোঅনুভলবসহায়োযারীঅেুগুললারঅনুসন্ধালনরিালঝপসইসক্ষিো

মনমহেরলয়লিযাোেিাোরোেএবংজলবায়ুেমরবেেনপিাযামবলায়উেলযাগীফসললরউৎোদনলয

েরামিেযরলেোরলব।

E

In their active state, phytochrome molecules bind themselves to DNA to restrict plant

growth. During the day, sunlight activates the molecules, slowing down growth. If a

plant finds itself in shade, phytochromes are quickly inactivated – enabling it to grow

Page 344 / 598

Page | 343

faster to find sunlight again. This is how plants compete to escape each other’s shade.

‘Light-driven changes to phytochrome activity occur very fast, in less than a second,’

says Wigge.

সমক্রয়থাযাঅবস্থায়সাইলিালক্রািঅেুসিূহমনলজলদরমিএনএরসালথপবঁলধপফললযালেযলরউমিলদর

বধেনলযআিযালনাযায়।মদলনরপবলায়সূলযেরআললাঅেুগুললালযসমক্রয়যলরবধেনলযযমিলয়পদয়।

যমদপযালনাগািমনলজলযিায়ারিলধেআমবষ্কারযলর, সাইলিালক্রািগুললােখনদ্রুেসমক্রয়হলয়ওলঠ

– এমিলযদ্রুেবধেলনসক্ষিযলরপোললযালেপফরসূলযেরআললাপখাঁজাযায়।এভালবইউমিলদরাএলয

অেলররিায়াপথলযপবমরলয়আসলেপ্রমেলযাগীোযরা।‘সাইলিালক্রালিরযাযেক্রলিআললাযোমলে

েমরবেেনখুবদ্রুেসংঘমিেহয়, এযপসলযলেরওযিসিলয়,’ উইগবলললিন।

At night, however, it’s a different story. Instead of a rapid deactivation following

sundown, the molecules gradually change from their active to inactive state. This is

called ‘dark reversion (প্রেোবেেন)’. ‘Just as mercury rises in a thermometer, the rate at

which phytochromes revert to their inactive state during the night is a direct measure of

temperature,’ says Wigge.

যমদওরালেএমিএযমিমভন্নগে।সূযোলস্তরেরএযমিদ্রুেগমেরমনমিয়োরবদললঅেুগুললাধীলর

ধীলরসমক্রয়পথলযমনমিয়অবস্থায়েমরবমেে

হয়।এমিলয‘অন্ধযালরপ্রেোবেেন’ বলল।‘পযিনভালব

োরদথালিোমিিালরবৃমিোয়, রালেসাইলিালক্রািপযহালরমনমিয়অবস্থায়প্রেোবমেে

হলবপসমি

োেিাোরএযমিসরাসমরেমরিাে,’ উইগআলরাবললন।

F

‘The lower the temperature, the slower the rate at which phytochromes revert to

inactivity, so the molecules spend more time in their active, growth-suppressing state.

This is why plants are slower to grow in winter. Warm temperatures accelerate dark

reversion, so that phytochromes rapidly reach an inactive state and detach themselves

from the plant’s DNA – allowing genes to be expressed and plant growth to resume.’

Wigge believes phytochrome thermo-sensing evolved at a later stage, and co-opted the

biological network already used for light-based growth during the downtime of night.

‘যেযিোেিাো, েেধীরগমেরহালরসাইলিালক্রািমনমিয়োয়প্রেোবমেে

হয়, অেএবঅেুগুললা

পবমিসিয়োলদরসমক্রয়, বধেনবান্ধবদিায়োরযলর।এযারলেইিীেযাললউমিদগুললাধীলরবৃমি

োয়।উষ্ণোেিাোঅন্ধযালরপ্রেোবেেনলযেরামিেযলরযালেযলরসাইলিালক্রািরাদ্রুেোরসালথ

G

Some plants mainly use day length as an indicator of the reason. Other species, such as

daffodils, have considerable temperature sensitivity, and can flower months in advance

during a warm winter. In fact, the discovery of the dual role of phytochromes provides

the science behind a well-known rhyme long used to predict the coming season: oak

before ash (এযধরলনরঅরলেেরবৃক্ষ) we’ll have a plash (োমনরঝােিা), ash before oak we’re

in for a soak (এলযবালরমভলজযাওয়া).

মযিুউমিদিূলেমদলনরবদঘেলযএইযারলেরএযমিসংলযেমহলসলববেবহারযলর।অনোনে

প্রজামেগুললাপযিনিোলফামিললরউলেখলযাগেোেিাোরপ্রমেসংলবদনিীলোরলয়লিএবংএযমিউষ্ণ

িীেযাললযলয়যিাসেূলবেইফুলমদলেোলর।এিনমযসাইলিালক্রালিরবিেভূমিযারআমবষ্কারেরবেেী

পি সুিসম্পলযেআনুিানযরারজনেদীঘেমদনধলরবেবহৃেএযমিঅমেেমরমেেিড়ারপেিলনরমবজ্ঞান

সম্পলযেধারোপ্রদানযলর: এলিরআলগওয, আিরাোলবাএযবৃমষ্টরঝােিা, ওলযরআলগএি,

আিরাএলযবালরমভলজযাওয়ারঅলেক্ষায়।

Wigge explains: ‘Oak trees rely much more on temperature, likely using phytochromes

as thermometers to dictate development, whereas ash trees rely on measuring day length

to determine their seasonal timing. A warmer spring, and consequently a higher

likeliness of a hot summer, will result in oak leafing before ash. A cold spring will see

the opposite. As the British know only too well, a colder summer is likely to be a rain-

soaked one.’

উইগবোখোযলরন: ‘ওযগািোেিাোরওেরপবমিমনভেরযলর, সম্ভবেসাইলিালক্রািলযথালিোমিিার

মহলসলববেবহারযলরবধেনলযমনলদেিপদয়, পযখালনএিগািোলদরপি সুমিসিয়যালমনধোরলেমদলনর

বদঘেিাোরওেরমনভেরযলর।এযমিউষ্ণবসন্তএবংেরবেেীলেএযমিউষ্ণিীলেরঅমধযসম্ভাবনা

েমরোলিএলিরআলগওলযোোগজালব।এযমিিীেলবসন্তএরউলিািাপদখলব।পযলহেুপযবল

মব্রমিিরাইজালনপযএযমিিীেলিীেহয়লোবাএযমিবৃমষ্টলভজাহলব।

H

The new findings are the culmination (েূড়ান্ত) of twelve years of research involving

scientists from Germany, Argentina and the US, as well as the Cambridge team. The

work was done in a model system, using a mustard plant called Arabidopsis, but Wigge

says the phytochrome genes necessary for temperature sensing are found in crop plants

as well. ‘Recent advances in plant genetics now mean that scientists are able to rapidly

identify the genes controlling these processes in crop plants, and even alter their activity

using precise molecular “scalpels”(িলেিুমলযা),’ adds Wigge. ‘Cambridge is uniquely

well-positioned to do this kind of research as we have outstanding collaborators nearby

who work on more applied aspects of plant biology, and can help us transfer this new

knowledge into the field.’

Cambridge-16, Test-4, Passage-1

Roman tunnels

কিামানিাগ্রনলসমূহ/সুিগপেসমূহ

The Romans, who once controlled areas of Europe, North Africa and Asia Minor,

adopted the construction techniques of other civilizations to build tunnels in their

territories

পরািানজামে, যারাএযসিয়ইউলরাে, উিরআমেযাএবংএমিয়াওইউলরালেরিলধেসংলযাগযারী

এলাযাসিূহমনয়িেযলরমিললা, মনলজলদরিামসেঅঞ্চললরপভেরিালনলমনিোলেঅনোনেসভেোর

মনিোেপয িলগুললালযিহেযলরমিললা

The Persians, who lived in present-day Iran, were one of the first civilizations to build

tunnels that provided a reliable supply of water to human settlements in dry areas. In the

early first millennium BCE, they introduced the qanat method of tunnel construction,

which consisted of placing posts over a hill in a straight line, to ensure that the tunnel

kept to its route, and then digging vertical shafts(এখালনখমনযূে) down into the ground at

regular intervals. Underground, workers removed the earth from between the ends of

the shafts, creating a tunnel. The excavated soil was taken up to the surface using the

shafts, which also provided ventilation during the work. Once the tunnel was completed,

it allowed water to flow from the top of a hillside down towards a canal, which supplied

Page 347 / 598

Page | 346

water for human use. Remarkably, some qanats built by the Persians 2,700 years ago

are still in use today.

োমসেয়ানরা, যারাআজলযরমদলনরইরালনবাসযরলো, প্রথিসভেোগুললারিলধেএযমিমিললাযারা

িালনলমনিোেযলরমিললাযাশুষ্কএলাযাগুললারিানববসমেগুললায়মনভেরলযাগেোমনরসরবরাহপ্রদান

যরলো।মিিেূবেপ্রথিিোব্দীলেোরািালনলমনিোলে‘যানাে’ েিমেরআমবভোবঘিায়, পযমিএযমি

োহালড়রওেরপসাজালসামজলাইলনপোিবসালনারিাধেলিগমঠেহলোযালেযলরমনমিেযরাযায়

পযিালনলমিোরেথধলররাখলিএবংেলরমনয়মিেবেবধালন/মবরমেলেখাড়াখামড়ভালবিামিরপভের

খমনযূেখননযরাহলো।িামিরমনলেযিেীরাখমনযূেগুললারপিষমদলযরিধেযারিামিগুললাসরালনার

িাধেলিিালনলবেমরযরলো।উিলনযৃেিামিগুললাখমনযূেগুললারিাধেলিভূেৃলষ্ঠরওেলরমনলয়আসা

হলোপযমিযাজেলাযাললবায়ুেলােললরবেবস্থাপ্রদানযরলো।এযবারিালনললরযাজপিষহলয়পগলল

এমিোমনলযোহালড়রেললরউেরহলেএযমিিালনললরমদলযপ্রবামহেহলেসাহাযেযরলোপযমি

িানববেবহালররজনেোমনরসরবরাহযরলো।উলেখলযাগেভালব, ২৭০০বিরআলগোমসেয়ানলদরবেমর

যরামযিুযানােএখলনাবেবহৃেহলে।

They later passed on their knowledge to the Romans, who also used the qanat method

to construct water-supply tunnels for agriculture. Roma qanat tunnels were constructed

with vertical shafts dug at intervals of between 30 and 60 meters. The shafts were

equipped with handholds and footholds to help those climbing in and out of them and

were covered with a wooden or stone lid. To ensure that the shafts were vertical, Romans

hung a plumb (প্রােীলররউলম্বোেরীক্ষারজনেসুলোয়বাঁধাসীসারখণ্ডবাবল) line from a rod

placed across the top of each shaft and made sure that the weight at the end of it hung in

the center of the shaft. Plumb lines were also used to measure the depth of the shaft and

to determine the slope of the tunnel. The 5.6-kilometer-long Claudius tunnel, built in 41

CE to drain the Fucine Lake in central Italy, had shafts that were up to 122 meters deep,

took 11 years to build and involved approximately 30,000 workers.

মযললামিিারগভীরপক্লওমিয়াসিালনললরএিনখমনযূেমিললাপযগুললা১২২মিিারেযেন্তগভীরমিললা,

পযগুললালযবানালে১১বিরপললগমিললাএবংআনুিামনয৩০,০০০যিেীএলেজমড়েমিললা।

By the 6th century BCE, a second method of tunnel construction appeared called

the counter-excavation method, in which the tunnel was constructed from both ends. It

was used to cut through high mountains when the qanat method was not a practical

alternative. This method required greater planning and advanced knowledge of

surveying, mathematics and geometry as both ends of a tunnel had to meet correctly at

the center of the mountain. Adjustments to the direction of the tunnel also had to be

made whenever builders encountered geological problems or when it deviated from its

set path. They constantly checked the tunnel’s advancing direction, for example, by

looking back at the light that penetrated through (পযালনামযিুরিধেমদলয়পোযালনা)the tunnel

mouth, and made corrections whenever necessary. Large deviations (মবেুেমে) could

happen, and they could result in one end of the tunnel not being usable. An inscription

(োথলরখমেে) written on the side of a 428-meter tunnel, built by the Romans as part of

the Saldae aqueduct system in modern-day Algeria, describes how the two teams of

builders missed each other in the mountain and how the later construction of a lateral

(োেেগে) link between both corridors corrected the initial error.

মিিেূবে৬ষ্ঠিোব্দীনাগাদোিা-খননেিমেনালিরিালনলমনিোলেরএযমিমিেীয়েিমেরআমবভোব

ঘলি, পযখালনউভয়প্রালন্তরপিষমদযপথলযইিালনলমনিোেযরাহলো।উেুঁোহাড়-েবেলেরিধেমদলয়

যািারজনেএবংযখনযানােেিমেএযমিবাস্তবসম্মেমবযেমিললানােখনএমিবেবহৃেহলো।

এইেিমেরজনেবড়ধরলনরেমরযেনাএবংসিীক্ষা, গমেেএবংজোমিমেযরারউচ্চেরজ্ঞালনর

The Romans dug tunnels for their roads using the counter-excavation method, whenever

they encountered obstacles such as hills or mountains that were too high for roads to

pass over. An example is the 37-meter-long, 6-meter-high, Furlo Pass Tunnel built in

Italy in 69-79 CE. Remarkably, a modern road still uses this tunnel today. Tunnels were

also built for mineral extraction. Miners would locate a mineral vein (আযমরলযবাখমনজ

েদালথেেূেেমিলারমেড়, ধােুমিরা) and then pursue it with shafts and tunnels underground.

Traces of such tunnels used to mine gold can still be found at the Dolaucothi mines in

Wales. When the sole purpose of a tunnel was mineral extraction, construction required

less planning, as the tunnel route was determined by the mineral vein.

আহরে, মনিোেযালযেযিেমরযেনারপ্রলয়াজনেড়লোপযলহেুিালনললরেথধােুমিরারিাধেলি

মনধোমরেহলো।

Roman tunnel projects were carefully planned and carried out. The length of time it took

to construct a tunnel depended on the method being used and the type of rock being

excavated. The qanat construction method was usually faster than the counter-

excavation method as it was more straightforward. This was because the mountain could

be excavated not only from the tunnel mouths but also from shafts. The type of rock

could also influence construction times.When the rock was hard, the Romans employed

a technique called fire quenching (োমনলেিুমবলয়পযালনামযিুলযঠাণ্ডাযরা) which consisted

of heating the rock with fire, and then suddenly cooling it with cold water so that it

would crack. Progress through hard rock could be very slow, and it was not uncommon

for tunnels to take years, if not decades, to be built. Construction marks left on a Roman

tunnel in Bologna show that the rate of advance through solid rock was 30 centimeters

per day. In contrast, the rate of advance of the Claudius tunnel can be calculated at 1.4

meters per day.Most tunnels had inscriptions showing the names of patrons who ordered

construction and sometimes the name of the architect. For example, the 1.4-kilometer

Çevlik tunnel in Turkey, built to divert the floodwater threatening the harbor (জাহালজর

পোোশ্রয়) of the ancient city of Seleuceia Pieria, had inscriptions on the entrance, still

visible today, that also indicate that the tunnel was started in 69 CE and was completed

in 81 CE.

changing and this has implications for everyone from the pre-reading toddler to the

expert adult.

সবাইলযসংযুক্তযলর: িমস্তলষ্করেড়ারক্ষিোরপেিলনদায়ীথাযাস্নায়মবযসামযেিমিঅমেসূক্ষ্মভালব

েমরবমেে

হলেএবংেড়লেনাোরাআড়াইবিলররবাচ্চাপথযঅমভজ্ঞপ্রাপ্তবয়স্কসবারওেরইএর

োৎেযেরলয়লি।

As work in neurosciences indicates, the acquisition(িহে/অজেন) of literacy necessitated

(অেোবমিেয/অেমরহাযেযলরপোলা) a new circuit in our species’ brain more than 6,000 years

ago. That circuit evolved from a very simple mechanism for decoding basic information,

like the number of goats in one’s herd, to the present, highly elaborated reading brain.

My research depicts (এখালনবেেনাযরা) how the present reading brain enables the

development of some of our most important intellectual and affective processes:

internalized knowledge, analogical reasoning, and inference; perspective-taking and

empathy; critical analysis and the generation of insight. Research surfacing in many

parts of the world now cautions that each of these essential ‘deep reading’ processes

may be under threat as we move into digital-based modes of reading.

মনউলরাসাইলন্সরগলবষোইমেেমদলেপয, অক্ষরজ্ঞালনরঅজেন৬০০০-এরওপবমিসিয়আলগআিালদর

প্রজামেরিমস্তলষ্কএযমিনেুনসামযেিলযঅেোবিযযলরপোলল।এইসামযেিমিপ্রাথমিযেযোলয়র

েথেলযমিলযািযরারজনেএযমিঅেেন্তসাধারেগঠনেিমেহলেমবযমিেহলয়লি, পযিনএযমি

েশুরোললথাযািাগললরসংখোপথলযআজলযরমদলনরেড়লেসক্ষিঅমেমবস্তৃেিমস্তষ্ক।আিার

গলবষোএখনসেযেযরলিপযএসযলঅেোবিেয‘মিেমরমিং’ প্রমক্রয়ারপ্রলেেযমিহয়লোহুিমযর

িুলখেড়লবপযলহেুআিরােড়ারজনে‘মিমজিাল-পবসি’/প্রযুমক্তমভমিযউোয়গুললায়স্থানান্তমরেহমে।

This is not a simple, binary issue of print versus digital reading and technological

innovations. As MIT scholar Sherry Turkle has written, we do not err (ভুলযরা) as a

society when we innovate but when we ignore what we disrupt or diminish while

innovating. In this hinge moment (এিনপযালনাসিয়বাঘিনাপযমিপযালনামযিুরসিাধালনঅমে

গুরুেেূেে) between print and digital cultures, society needs to confront what is

diminishing in the expert reading circuit, what our children and older students are not

developing, and what we can do about it.

এমিএযমিসাধারেমপ্রন্টবনািমিমজিালমরমিংএবংপ্রযুমক্তগেআমবষ্কালররবিেসিসোনয়।পযিনিা

এিআইমিেমণ্ডেপিমরিাযেলমললখলিন, আিরাএযমিসিাজমহলসলবভুলযমরনাযখনআিরাআমবষ্কার

েখন(মঠযইমবষয়মিভুললরিলধেেলড়)।মপ্রন্টএবংমিমজিালসংস্কৃমেরিধেযারএইগুরুেেূেেমবন্দুলে

সিালজরলযানমজমনসমিদক্ষমরমিংসামযলিেরিলধেক্ষয়প্রাপ্তহলে, পযানমজমনসগুললারআিালদরবাচ্চারা

এবংবয়স্কমিক্ষাথেীরামবযািসাধনযরলিনাএবংআিরাএমনলয়যীযরলেোমর- পসসলবরসম্মুখীন

হওয়াপ্রলয়াজন।

We know from research that the reading circuit is not given to human beings through a

genetic blueprint like vision or language; it needs an environment to develop. Further,

it will adapt to that environment’s requirements – from different writing systems to the

characteristics of whatever medium is used. If the dominant medium advantages

processes that are fast, multi-task oriented and well-suited(উেযুক্ত) for large volumes of

information, like the current digital medium, so will the reading circuit. As UCLA

psychologist Patricia Greenfield writes, the result is that less attention and time will be

allocated to slower, time-demanding deep reading processes.

গলবষোপথলযআিরাজামনপযমরমিংসামযেিিানুষলযদৃমষ্টিমক্তবাভাষারিলোমজনগেনীলনযিার

িাধেলিপ্রদানযরাহয়মন; এরমবযালিরজনেএযমিেমরলবলিরপ্রলয়াজনেলড়।আবার, এমিেমরলবলির

োমহদাঅনুযায়ীঅমভলযামজেহয়– মবমভন্নধরলনরপলখারধরনপথলযশুরুযলরপযিাধেিবেবহারযরা

মললখলিন, ফলাফলিাহলেযিিলনালযাগএবংসিয়িুযুধীরগমের, সিয়-সালেক্ষমিেমরমিংপ্রমক্রয়ার

জনেবরাদ্দহলব।

Increasing reports from educators and from researchers in psychology and the

humanities bear this out (পযালনামযিুরসেেলযসিথেনযরা). English literature scholar and

teacher Mark Edmundson describes how many college students actively avoid the

classic literature of the 19th and 20th centuries in favour of something simpler as they

no longer have the patience to read longer, denser, more difficult texts. We should be

less concerned with students’ ‘cognitive impatience’, however, than by what may

underlie it: the potential inability of large numbers of students to read with a level of

critical analysis sufficient to comprehend (উেলমিযরা/পবাঝা) the complexity of thought

and argument found in more demanding texts.

িলনামবজ্ঞানওিানমবযমবষয়যমিক্ষামবদএবংগলবষযলদরপথলযপ্রাপ্তবাড়লেথাযামরলোিেসিূহএই

মবেরীলে/েুলনায়এরিূললযীলসরপ্রভাবরলয়লি: মবেুলসংখোয়মিক্ষাথেীলদরজমিলমবলেষেপযমি

আলরাপবমিোমহদাসম্পন্নপলখনীগুললায়প্রাপ্তমেন্তাএবংযুমক্তরজমিলোলযপবাঝার/উেলমিযরারজনে

যলথষ্টপসমিেড়লেোরারসম্ভাবেদক্ষোহীনো।

Multiple studies show that digital screen use may be causing a variety of troubling

downstream effects(পযমজমনলসরপ্রভাবেরবেেীলেওপদখামদলব) on reading comprehension

(উেলমিযরারক্ষিো) in older high school and college students. In Stavanger, Norway,

psychologist Anne Mangen and colleagues studied how high school students

comprehend the same material in different mediums. Mangen’s group asked subjects

questions about a short story whose plot had universal student appeal; half of the

students read the story on a tablet, the other half in paperback. Results indicated that

students who read on print were superior in their comprehension to screen-reading

peers, particularly in their ability to sequence (অনুক্রি/েরম্পরা) detail and reconstruct the

plot in chronological (যালানুক্রমিয) order.

মবমভন্নিাধেলিএযইমজমনসলযউেলমিযলর।িোনলজলনরদলেরীক্ষেোেলদরএযমিপিািগে

সম্পলযেপ্রেযলরনপযমিরেিভূমিরসাবেজনীনভালবমিক্ষাথেীলদরিালঝিহেলযাগেোমিললা; অলধেয

মিক্ষাথেীরাএযমিিোবলললিগেমিোঠযলর, বামযঅলধেযযাগলজরবইলয়পসমিেলড়।ফলাফলইমেে

পদয়পয, পযসবমিক্ষাথেীরামপ্রন্টযমেমিেলড়লি, মিলনেড়াদললরেুলনায়োলদরউেলমিরবোোলর

অমধযেরভাললামিললা, মবলিষযলরবেেনারঅনুক্রিএবংেিভূমিমিলযযালানুক্রলিেুনগেঠলনরপক্ষলে

োলদরদক্ষোরবোোলর।

Ziming Liu from San Jose State University has conducted a series of studies which

indicate that the ‘new norm (আদিে)’ in reading is skimming (পোখবুমললয়যাওয়া), involving

word-spotting and browsing (েুলরাপলখানােলড়পযালনাবইবািোগামজলনপোখপবালালনা)

through the text. Many readers now use a pattern when reading in which they sample

the first line and then word-spot through the rest of the text. When the reading brain

skims like this, it reduces time allocated to deep reading processes. In other words, we

don’t have time to grasp complexity, to understand another’s feelings, to perceive

beauty, and to create thoughts of the reader’s own. The possibility that critical analysis,

empathy and other deep reading processes could become the unintended ‘collateral

(এযইউৎসহলেউিূে) damage’ of our digital culture is not a straightforward binary issue

about print versus digital reading. It is about how we all have begun to read o various

mediums and how that changes not only what we read, but also the purposes for which

we read. Nor is it only about the young. The subtle (সূক্ষ্ম) atrophy (ক্ষয়,ক্ষময়ঞ্চুো) of critical

analysis and empathy affects us all equally. It affects our ability to navigate a constant

bombardment (পগালাবষে) of information. It incentivizes (প্রলোমদেযরা) a retreat to the

most familiar stores of unchecked information, which require and receive no analysis,

leaving us susceptible (সংলবদনিীল) to false information and irrational (অলয মক্তয) ideas.

বিেঘিনানয়।এমিআিরাসবাইযীভালবমবমভন্নিাধেলিেড়লেশুরুযলরমিপসমিসম্পলযেএবং

উলদ্দিেসিূহওেমরবেেনযলর।এমিপযবলপিালিালদরবোোলরইনয়।জমিল/ সিাললােনািূলযমবলেষে

এবংসহানুভূমেরএইসূক্ষক্ষময়ঞ্চুোআিালদরসযললযইসিানলযপ্রভামবেযলর।এমিেলথেরএযমি

ধারাবামহযপগালাবষেলযেমরোলনায়আিালদরসক্ষিোলযপ্রভামবেযলর।এমিঅযাোইযৃেেলথের

সবলেলয়েমরমেেভাণ্ডারলযএযমিেিাৎেসরেলযপ্রলোমদেযলর, পযগুললাপযালনামবলেষেিহেযলর

নাবাপসমিরপ্রলয়াজনেলড়না, যাআিালদরলযমিথোেথেএবংঅলয মক্তযধারোরপ্রমেসংলবদনিীল

যলরপোলল।

There’s an old rule in neuroscience that does not alter with age: use it or lose it. It is a

very hopeful principle when applied to critical thought in the reading brain because it

implies choice. The story of the changing reading brain is hardly finished. We possess

(বলিরাখা) both the science and the technology to identify and redress (প্রমেযারযরা) the

changes in how we read before they become entrenched (দৃঢ়ভালবস্থামেেহওয়া). If we

work to understand exactly what we will lose, alongside the extraordinary new

capacities that the digital world has brought us, there is as much reason for excitement

as caution.

স্নায়ুমবজ্ঞালনএযমিেুলরালনামনয়িরলয়লিপযমিসিলয়রসালথবদলায়না: বেবহারযলরাবাহামরলয়

পফললা।এমিএযমিপবিআিাবাদীনীমেযখনমরমিংপব্রইলনজমিলমবলেষলেরবেবহারযরাহয়যারে

এরিলধেেিন্দমনমহে।মরমিংপব্রইলনরেমরবেেলনরঘিনাপিষহয়মনবলললইেলল।আিরামবজ্ঞান

ওপ্রযুমক্তরউভয়মিলযইমনলজলদরবলিপরলখমিযালেযলরআিরাযীভালবেমড়পসখালনআসা

েমরবেেনগুললালযদৃঢ়ভালবস্থামেেহবারআলগইমেমিেএবংপ্রমেযারযরাযায়।

Cambridge-16, Test-4, Passage-3

Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence

যৃমেিবুমিিিারপ্রমেিলনাভাব

A

Page 356 / 598

Page | 355

Artificial intelligence (AI) can already predict the future. Police forces are using it to

map when and where crime is likely to occur. Doctors can use it to predict when a patient

is most likely to have a heart attack or stroke. Researchers are even trying to give AI

imagination so it can plan for unexpected consequences.

যৃমেিবুমিিিাইলোিলধেভমবষেেলযঅনুিানযরলেোলর।আইনিৃঙ্খলারক্ষাযারীবামহনীগুললাযখন

এবংপযাথায়অেরাধহয়লোবাঘিলেেলললিপসমিরিানমেেবেমরলেবেবহারযরলি।মেমযৎসযরা

এযজনপরাগীযখনহািেঅোিাযবাপস্ট্রাযহওয়ারসবলেলয়পবমিসম্ভাবেোরিলধেরলয়লিনোঅনুিান

যরলেবেবহারযরলেোলরন।এিনমযগলবষযরাএআইলযযেনািক্তুপদওয়ারপেষ্টাযরলিনযালে

যলরএমিঅনাযামঙ্ক্ষেফলাফলসিূহসম্পলযেেমরযেনাযরলেোলর।

Many decisions in our lives require a good forecast, and AI is almost always better at

forecasting than we are. Yet for all these technological advances, we still seem to deeply

lack confidence in AI predictions. Recent cases show that people don’t like relying on

AI and prefer to trust human experts, even if these experts are wrong.

আিালদরজীবলনরঅলনযমসিালন্তরএযমিভাললােূবোভালসরপ্রলয়াজনেলড়এবংযৃমেিবুমিিিাপ্রায়

সবসিয়ইআিালদরপেলয়ভাললাভালবেূবোভাসপবরযলর।যমদওএসযলপ্রযুমক্তগেঅিগমেরেরও

আিরাপযনএখলনাএআইলয়রঅনুিালনরপ্রমেগভীরভালবআত্মমবোলসরঅভাবপবাধযমর।সাম্প্রমেয

ঘিনাগুললাপদখালেপযিানুষএআইলয়রওেরমনভেরযরলেেিন্দযলরনাএবংিানুষমবলিষজ্ঞলদর

মবোসযরািাপবমিেিন্দযলরএিনমযযমদওএসযলমবলিষজ্ঞরাভুলহন।

If we want AI to really benefit people, we need to find a way to get people to trust it. To

do that, we need to understand why people are so reluctant to trust AI in the first place.

আিরাযমদোইপযএআইবাস্তলবইিানুষলযউেযৃেযরুয, আিালদরলযিানুষলযএমিরপ্রমেমবোস

যরালেএযমিউোয়খুঁজলেহলব।এিনমিযরলেহললআিালদরলযবুঝলেহলবপ্রথিেপযনিানুষজন

এআইলয়রওেরমবোসযলরঅনািহী?

B

Take the case of Watson for Oncology, one of technology giant IBM’s supercomputer

programs. Their attempt to promote this program to cancer doctors was a PR disaster

(PR=public relation, বেবসাসম্পলযেএিনএযপনমেবােযঘিনাবাসিাললােনাযাজনিানুলষর

িলধেমনন্দারমিযারহয়). The AI promised to deliver top-quality recommendations on the

treatment of 12 cancers that accounted for 80% of the world’s cases. But when doctors

first interacted with Watson, they found themselves in a rather difficult situation. On

the one hand, if Watson provided guidance about a treatment that coincided (মিললযাওয়া)
